claims.claim: Under Art. 4(2) of the US–Netherlands treaty a US citizen who is not Dutch, has lived there under 7 of the last 10 years and had no clear intention to stay may be treated as US-domiciled
claims.oldWording: has lived there under 7 of the last 10 years and had no clear intention to stay may be treated
claims.newWording: has lived there under 7 of the last 10 years, was there for business, study, tourism or a similar purpose and had no clear intention to stay may be treated as US-domiciled (a retiree who settles may not fit; check with an adviser)

sources.name: Inview (Wolters Kluwer): US–Netherlands estate tax convention, Article 4
sources.says: Article 4(2): a decedent who was a citizen of one State and not the other, and domiciled in both under paragraph 1, "shall be deemed to have been domiciled in (and only in) the State of which he was a citizen, if" (a) he had been domiciled in the other State "in the aggregate less than 7 years during the 10-year period ending at his death"; and (b) he was there "for business, professional, educational, training, tourism, or a similar purpose" (or as the spouse or dependant of such a person) "and did not have a clear intention to remain indefinitely in the other State." Trb. 1969, 221; in force 03-02-1971.

also: summary unchanged: "(the US estate treaty may limit this for shorter stays)" is still hedged with "may"
claims.note: The article has two conditions joined by "and"; the profile gave the years and the intention but left out the purpose of the stay, which is the one a retiree may fail. Whether retirement is a "similar purpose" is not something a page read settles.

claims.claim: The treaty otherwise gives credit relief

sources.name: Inview (Wolters Kluwer): US–Netherlands estate tax convention, Article 11
sources.says: Article 11(1): where both States tax property covered by Article 6 or 7, the State taxing on domicile or citizenship "shall allow a credit equal to the amount of the tax imposed by the other State." 11(2)(a): for other property, where the decedent was a citizen of one State and had been domiciled in the other for 7 or more of the last 10 years, "the State of which he was a citizen shall allow a credit equal to the amount of the tax imposed by such other State."
